newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-N.Express boosts bus and train profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-N.Express boosts bus and train profits.

text.p: British transport operator National Express announced a 45 percent jump in profits on Thursday and said it was now looking for opportunities to take over public transport services in mainland Europe.
Group pretax profits rose to 60.1 million pounds ($96.3 million) last year from 41.5 million in 1995 on sales up 51 percent at 482.5 million pounds.
The year's total dividend payout was increased 1.5 pence to 11.5p a share on earnings up 17.5 percent at 32.8 pence.
Operating profits at the company's bus division jumped 59 percent to 39.4 million pounds on sales of 175.59 million pounds last year, boosted by further acquisitions.

The Express Coaches division made an operating profit of 10.48 million pounds on sales of 169.87 million pounds, while its East Midlands Airport in Britain made 10.3 million pounds on turnover of 28.62 million pounds.
"We are looking around Europe at the moment in terms of buses, coaches, airports and trains, and watching closely and trying to get in early," chief executive Phil White said in an interview.
"There are targets in sight but I want to keep them to myself at the moment," he said.
"They (other European governments) seem to be a bit behind the UK but they are certainly moving towards a more deregulated, privatised system."

The company only moved into rail services last year but now ranks as one of Britain's largest operators, having won five of the 25 passenger service franchises awarded by the British government under its controversial privatisation of the national rail network.
Franchisees are now on test to prove to politicians and passengers opposed to the break-up of the former British Rail network that they can improve services.

White said he was confident he could work with the opposition Labour Party if it wins the May 1 general election, and saw no comparisons with rival bus and trains operator Stagecoach Holdings Plc which has been heavily criticised for its management of the South West Trains (SWT) franchise.

Shares in Stagecoach, a former darling of the stock market, have plunged this month after SWT enraged passengers by cancelling hundreds of services on its commuter lines into London because staff cuts had left it short of drivers.
Stagecoach shares had fallen a further 52 pence to 640 by 1345 GMT on Thursday, against a year high of 804. National Express was off 5-1/2 at 525-1/2 against a year high of 581.

White said Stagecoach's problems could have been avoided. National Express has cut its own workforce by 20 percent to around 1,170 staff on its Midland Mainline and Gatwick Express franchises since they were taken over.
"Done in the right way, you should not have any problems and certainly we haven't," he told Reuters.

"We talk to a lot of politicians," he said. "We think we have got a feeling as to what they want and at the end of the day if it is a Labour government I think they are more interested in quality than going back to the old network with its high subsidies which will cost them a fortune."
If the franchise operators showed themselves willing to reinvest profits, he said he believed a Labour government would be well pleased.
The firm said Midland Mainline and Gatwick Express made 2.097 million pounds in operating profits on 108.48 million pounds of income in their eight months with National Express last year.

Passenger traffic on Midland Mainline increased by nine percent last year, while Gatwick Express, which operates the fast rail link between central London and Gatwick Airport, saw a three percent increase in passengers.
This year the company has been awarded a further three train franchises, Scotrail, Central Trains and North London Railways.
